In this VladTV sit-down, Harlem rapper G. Dep reflects on his early years before Bad Boy Records, “Special Delivery,” and “Let’s Get It.” Born to a young mother and raised between Washington Heights and Harlem’s James Weldon Johnson Projects, he recalls coming of age as crack reshaped New York street life in the late ’80s and early ’90s. G. Dep discusses finding a gun as a kid, seeing figures like Rich Porter, Azie Faison, and Alpo Martinez in the neighborhood, and how flashy cars, jewelry, and fast money influenced teenagers around him. He also opens up about selling drugs at 13 or 14, making “get fresh money,” avoiding heavier drug use, and navigating street politics as a young man. The conversation adds context to his later Bad Boy career and the 2010 police confession tied to a 1993 murder case.

Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev breaks down how the trading app rebounded after a brutal 2022–2023 downturn, with shares now roughly 15x above their lowest point. In this conversation, Tenev explains how COVID-era stimulus checks, zero interest rates, inflation, Federal Reserve rate hikes, and the post-pandemic reopening reshaped investor behavior and hit growth stocks across the market. He also discusses why many IPO-era companies stayed below their offering price while Robinhood used the difficult period to expand beyond stock trading.

Tenev details the company’s push into retirement accounts, high-yield products, Robinhood Gold, active trader tools, banking-style features, and services for high-net-worth customers. Vlad also reflects on his own portfolio losses during the 2022 S&P 500 decline and the rebound that followed. The interview offers insight into Robinhood’s long-term vision to become a global financial platform and “financial home” for everyday investors.

Memo600 sits down with Vlad to break down his rapid rise in Chicago drill after coming home in 2016 and stepping into music almost by accident. He recalls going viral from YouTube trolling, getting encouragement from a cameraman connected to his family, and turning that momentum into early records like “Steppers” and “Exposing Me.” Memo explains how King Von later jumped on the “Exposing Me” remix, helping push the movement even further.

The interview also details how Lil Durk, known as Smurk, approached him about joining OTF while Memo was still loyal to Team 600. He discusses Just Blow being part of the deal, their short-lived Chop Squad situation with Young Chop in Atlanta, contract issues, lawyers, chains, studio time, and making $30,000 to $50,000 a month from shows. Memo reflects on going from prison conversations to touring and motivating others.

Poetik Flakko sits down with Vlad for a wide-ranging conversation on hip hop, internet sleuthing, street violence, and the real-life costs of online fame. The discussion opens with Vlad reflecting on how social media now shapes narratives around crimes in rap, including the Q50 case, Chicago artists, and examples involving Common and Twista, before debating vigilante justice through the Clark Fredericks case.

Flakko then breaks down his unlikely path to No Jumper: leaving North Dakota in 2022, driving 27 hours to Los Angeles in a 2011 Chevy Malibu with a cracked windshield and $300, after telling Adam22 he already lived in L.A. He recalls booking a shared Airbnb, landing a $6,000-a-month contract through Josh, and going from $12-an-hour document processing work to becoming an on-air host. Flakko also explains why Reddit backlash, harassment, health goals, and peace of mind led him to step away.

--------
In this VladTV full interview, Vincent “Gigi” Marino, a former Patriarca crime family soldier from Boston and Revere, recounts his path from aspiring Massachusetts state trooper to armed robber, Mafia associate, and federal inmate. Marino discusses his Italian roots, early stickups, bank robberies in Boston’s North End, and the rise of the New England Mafia under Raymond Patriarca Sr. and Raymond Patriarca Jr. He details the violent 1980s–90s power struggle involving Frank Salemme, Joseph Russo, Vincent “The Animal” Ferrara, Whitey Bulger, Stevie Flemmi, and FBI agent John Connolly, including the 1989 IHOP shooting and the RICO case that led to a 35-year sentence. After serving 28 years, Marino reflects on prison politics, Fort Dix, Whitey Bulger’s killing, legal work behind bars, and life after release as an author and filmmaker with Patriarca Purge. A rare firsthand account of Boston organized crime, federal corruption claims, and survival.

Carlos Lehder reflects on the early days before his connection to Pablo Escobar, including his 1976 partnership with “Boston George” and the events surrounding Escobar’s arrest by the Colombian Security Service with 39 kilos of cocaine. In this VladTV interview, Lehder explains how Escobar’s cousin, Gustavo, introduced him to the future Medellín Cartel boss and recalls selling cars to him after the infamous arrest, trial, alleged judge bribery, and the later killing of the agent involved.

Lehder also shares his view of Escobar’s rise from the barrios of Medellín, describing a violent youth marked by crime before Escobar realized the enormous profits in cocaine trafficking. The conversation offers rare firsthand commentary on how Pablo Escobar began moving into the cocaine trade, his early mistakes, and the ruthless reputation that followed him long before he became one of Colombia’s most notorious figures.

recentItems.description:

Part 1: https://youtu.be/W6Vqal8IQfk
--------
William Noguera sits down with Vlad to recount going to trial in California for the murder of his girlfriend’s mother and facing the death penalty as a young defendant in the late 1980s. He explains why no plea deal was offered, how his attorney assessed the risk, and what it felt like knowing execution was possible before Robert Alton Harris became California’s first execution in 1992. Noguera discusses the prosecution’s case, including alleged circumstantial evidence, a key witness, insurance money claims, and his accusations involving cop Kirby Keltner. He also reflects on how an alibi witness unraveled after pressure from the DA, damaging his defense. The interview breaks down the jury’s first-degree murder conviction, special circumstances finding, and California’s penalty phase, where jurors chose between life without parole and death. Noguera describes the moment the jury returned with a death sentence after just minutes of deliberation.
